# Miller GEQDSK generation

## Miller generator

[gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.py](gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.py) is both an importable module and a command-line
generator. It requires NumPy and SciPy. Matplotlib is optional, for `--plot`.
The implementation plan is [MILLER_EQDSK_PLAN.md](MILLER_EQDSK_PLAN.md); all formulas and numerical
methods are documented in [gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.tex](gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.tex).

From the repository root:

```bash
python3 gyrokinetic/data/eqdsk/miller/gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.py \
  gyrokinetic/data/eqdsk/miller/miller_tcv.py --output tcv_miller.geqdsk \
  --nr 257 --nz 257 --plot tcv_miller.png
```

The Python input defines `geometry={...}` and a scalar `q(R_omp)` function. All
physical parameters belong in that file; the CLI never evaluates a function
expression. `R_omp` is outboard midplane MAJOR radius in meters. Required geometry
keys are `R_axis`, `B_axis` (toroidal field), and `R_lcfs` (outboard LCFS major radius).
Defaults: `Z_axis=0`, `kappa=1`, `delta=0`, `a_shift=0`. Lengths are meters and fields
tesla. The initial convention requires positive `B_axis` and positive finite q.

Optional `R_omp_bounds=(lower,upper)` requests coverage of complete flux surfaces
for a core annulus, SOL-only simulation, or LCFS-crossing simulation. These are
NOT rectangular R bounds. The equilibrium always includes the axis and LCFS;
q must be valid all the way from the axis through the physical guard surface.
Without coverage bounds the LCFS is the outer certified surface. `--rz-bounds RMIN RMAX ZMIN ZMAX` explicitly sets the rectangular grid but does not extend
the certified physical surfaces. Rectangular corners use the documented smooth
flux continuation beyond the guard, identified in the JSON summary and plots.
The default 5-percent guard needs at least three R-Z cells of clearance; coarse
grids may require `--guard-fraction 0.25`. The node counts must be odd, 5..999.

The output includes `<output>.json`, with parameters, input provenance, flux
values, physical coverage, a conversion table, and numerical residuals. The
GEQDSK has constant `F=R_axis*B_axis` and zero pressure/current placeholders. It is
a synthetic magnetic geometry, not a Grad-Shafranov solution or a wall model.
No limiter is written. The existing tokamak IWL machinery supplies wall cuts.

Examples [miller_d3d.py](miller_d3d.py) and [miller_tcv.py](miller_tcv.py) preserve their corresponding analytic
regression inputs' surfaces and q profiles. TCV uses the actual shifted `r(x)`
endpoint surfaces, not its nominal `Rmid` bounds. Read it with `reflect=false` to
preserve `Z_axis`. LTX replaces the old rational q profile (pole at `R_omp` about
0.688328 m) with a positive exponential profile preserving LCFS q and shear.
The original script and data file remain available for comparison.

### Python API

```python
from gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk import (
  MillerGeometry, MillerEquilibrium, sample_eqdsk, write_eqdsk)
geometry = MillerGeometry(R_axis=2, B_axis=1.5, R_lcfs=2.5)
equilibrium = MillerEquilibrium(geometry, lambda R_omp: 2)
data = sample_eqdsk(equilibrium)
write_eqdsk("circle.geqdsk", equilibrium, data)
print(equilibrium.coordinates(2.4))  # R_omp, Miller r, psi, rho_psi, q.
```

### Verification

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s gyrokinetic/data/eqdsk/miller -v
make -j6 LIBRARY_TARGET=library gyrokinetic
make -j6 build/gyrokinetic/unit/ctest_gen_miller_eqdsk
./build/gyrokinetic/unit/ctest_gen_miller_eqdsk
```

Use no more than half the available processors for make. To exercise the native
reader on Python outputs as well, generate files named miller_ltx.geqdsk,
miller_d3d.geqdsk, and miller_tcv.geqdsk in one directory, then run the same C
test with `GKYL_MILLER_REFERENCE_DIR` set to that directory. Native tests always
construct their own temporary fixtures, so normal unit runs need no Python.
Both quadratic and cubic reconstructions are checked; full geometry creation
uses the existing quadratic tokamak path. LaTeX can be checked with:

```bash
pdflatex -halt-on-error -output-directory=/tmp \
  gyrokinetic/data/eqdsk/miller/gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.tex
```

## Native updater and app API

[gkyl_gen_miller_eqdsk.h](../../../zero/gkyl_gen_miller_eqdsk.h) exposes `_inew`, `_advance`, `_write`, `_get_info`,
`_psi_from_omp`, `_omp_from_psi`, `_surface`, and `_release`. Its `qprofile` callback takes
`(double R_omp, void *ctx)`. The native angular quadrature uses periodic
trapezoidal refinement with an explicit convergence test; radial interpolation
and the rectangular continuation follow the Python reference. It is a host
initialization updater, with no CUDA or MPI dependency.

The app accepts `geometry.geometry_id=GKYL_GEOMETRY_MILLER` and parameters in
`geometry.miller_grid_info`, of type `struct gkyl_gen_miller_eqdsk_inp`. In this mode
app `lower[0]` and `upper[0]` are outboard major radii. Initialization resolves the
mutable input IN PLACE to psi bounds and `GKYL_GEOMETRY_TOKAMAK`, before creating
the configuration grid. Solver callbacks therefore receive the ordinary
tokamak coordinates (psi, alpha, parallel coordinate). They do not receive the
old analytic input's (x,y,theta). Use the updater conversions when migrating
physical profiles. Binormal extents and parallel coordinates use the existing
tokamak conventions; arbitrary analytic-input callbacks cannot be reused
without their coordinate transformations.

Generation writes `<app-name>-miller.geqdsk` unless `geometry.efit_info.filepath` is
set. Rank zero writes, collective status handling precedes reading, and the
file is retained. Generation parameters are recorded in geometry metadata.
The q callback must be deterministic and identical on all ranks. Initialization
regenerates the file, including before a restart; there is no cached-file reuse
mode. Keep the same geometry and q inputs when restarting a simulation.
The app selects IWL geometry, disables reflection, and derives R-Z search bounds.
It supports single-block 2x/3x domains, excluding the coordinate singularity at
the magnetic axis. Multiblock and language-binding APIs are not provided here.

An LCFS crossing sets `has_LCFS` and must align with a psi cell face. No requested
domain surfaces are moved; mismatch beyond GEQDSK serialization precision
causes initialization to fail. `x_LCFS` is represented by the matching grid face;
the wall cutoff uses the serialized boundary flux. Core-only and SOL-only
domains have no internal split. Set ordinary species BCs: twist-shift for a
3x core annulus, and the desired open-line BCs for SOL/crossing cases. The app's
existing mixed-domain machinery handles the core part of a crossing.

The focused regression `rt_gk_miller_3x2v_p1` constructs all three domains and
advances each by one step. It uses constant profiles and a static zero field
to isolate geometry/BC initialization. Run in a scratch directory to contain
its output; MPI partitions the parallel (third configuration) direction:

```bash
make -j6 build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_miller_3x2v_p1
./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_miller_3x2v_p1 -s1
<MPI-prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 2 \
  ./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_miller_3x2v_p1 -M -e2 -s1
```

Check the returned app pointer for `NULL` after a Miller initialization failure.
\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb,booktabs,geometry,hyperref}
\geometry{margin=1in}
\title{Synthetic Miller GEQDSK generation in Gkeyll}
\author{Gkeyll}
\date{}
\newcommand{\Ra}{R_{\mathrm{axis}}}
\newcommand{\Za}{Z_{\mathrm{axis}}}
\newcommand{\Romp}{R_{\mathrm{omp}}}
\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section{Purpose, inputs, and conventions}
The module \texttt{gkeyll\_gen\_miller\_eqdsk.py} constructs a synthetic
axisymmetric magnetic geometry for the existing Gkeyll tokamak reader.
Prescribed surfaces and safety factor determine poloidal flux, with constant
$F=RB_\phi$. These choices do not in general solve the Grad--Shafranov equation.
The GEQDSK pressure, pressure derivative, and current fields are zero
placeholders; the physical wall is not specified.

Lengths are in meters and magnetic fields in tesla. The flux $\psi$ is poloidal
flux divided by $2\pi$, in Wb/radian. We set $\psi_{\rm axis}=0$, with positive
$B_{\rm axis}$ and $q$ and flux increasing outward. The input function
$q(\Romp)$ takes the major radius at the outboard midplane, in meters.
The Miller surface label $r$ is a minor radius, whereas $R$ is the cylindrical
major radius at an arbitrary poloidal position.

Required parameters are $\Ra$, $B_{\rm axis}$, and the outboard LCFS major
radius. Defaults are $\Za=0$, $\kappa=1$, $\delta=0$, and $A=0$, where
$A$ denotes \texttt{a\_shift}. Optional outboard midplane bounds identify
complete flux surfaces intended for a simulation. They are independent of
the rectangular mesh bounds and do not crop the equilibrium to an annulus.
Core annuli, SOL-only regions, and LCFS-crossing regions are all possible.
Miller surfaces themselves contain no diverted X-point; the IWL infrastructure
supplies wall cuts for the open-field-line portion of a simulation.

\section{Surface map and analytic derivatives}
Define $\eta=\arcsin\delta$ and $h=\theta+\eta\sin\theta$. Then
\begin{align}
R(r,\theta)&=\Ra-\frac{Ar^2}{2\Ra}+r\cos h, &
Z(r,\theta)&=\Za+\kappa r\sin\theta,\\
R_r&=-\frac{Ar}{\Ra}+\cos h, &
R_\theta&=-r(1+\eta\cos\theta)\sin h,\\
Z_r&=\kappa\sin\theta, & Z_\theta&=\kappa r\cos\theta.
\end{align}
Let $D=R_rZ_\theta-R_\theta Z_r$. The cylindrical volume Jacobian is
$J_r=RD$. A useful regular expression is
\begin{equation}
\frac{D}{r}=\kappa\left[
\left(\cos h-\frac{Ar}{\Ra}\right)\cos\theta
+(1+\eta\cos\theta)\sin h\sin\theta\right].
\end{equation}
The implementation checks positive $R$ and $D/r$ on sampled physical surfaces,
including the limiting value at the axis. It also checks that the outboard
midplane map remains increasing. These numerical checks cannot prove validity
of an arbitrary user function between all sampled points.

At $\theta=0$,
\begin{equation}
\Romp(r)=\Ra-\frac{Ar^2}{2\Ra}+r,\qquad
\frac{d\Romp}{dr}=1-\frac{Ar}{\Ra}.
\end{equation}
For $d=\Romp-\Ra$, its stable increasing-branch inverse is
\begin{equation}
r=\frac{2d}{1+\sqrt{1-2Ad/\Ra}}.
\end{equation}
This expression includes the $A=0$ limit without cancellation. The LCFS
radius $a$ is obtained by applying it to the specified LCFS major radius.
A nonzero shift changes the horizontal surface center with radius; it is
independent of the constant vertical offset $\Za$.

Set $F=\Ra B_{\rm axis}$. In cylindrical coordinates the field convention is
\begin{equation}
B_R=-\frac{\psi_Z}{R},\qquad B_Z=\frac{\psi_R}{R},\qquad B_\phi=\frac{F}{R}.

\psi_R=\psi'(r)\frac{Z_\theta}{D},\qquad
\psi_Z=-\psi'(r)\frac{R_\theta}{D},\qquad
B_p=\frac{\psi'(r)}{RD}\sqrt{R_\theta^2+Z_\theta^2}.
\end{equation}
The toroidal turns per poloidal circuit give
\begin{equation}
q(r)=\frac{F}{2\pi\psi'(r)}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{D}{R}\,d\theta.
\end{equation}
Consequently the imposed safety factor determines
\begin{equation}
\psi'(r)=\frac{F}{2\pi q(\Romp(r))}
\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{D}{R}\,d\theta.
\end{equation}
The boundary flux is $\psi_b=\psi(a)$, and
$\rho_\psi=\sqrt{\psi/\psi_b}$, including values above one in the physical SOL.
The profile must be defined from the axis through the guard, even when the
simulation begins away from the axis.

\section{Radial quadrature and interpolation}
Use $s=r^2$. With $g(s)=d\psi/ds$, the regular quadrature is
\begin{equation}
g(s)=\frac{F}{4\pi\Ra q(\Romp(\sqrt{s}))}
\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{\Ra}{R}\frac{D}{r}\,d\theta.
\end{equation}
The integrand is dimensionless and has a finite limit at $s=0$. A constant
triangularity extended to the axis can introduce $\sqrt{s}$ terms into $g$;
finiteness does not imply an analytic Taylor series in $s$ or a smooth axis
Hessian of $\psi(R,Z)$ for general triangular shapes.

SciPy adaptive quadrature evaluates the integral with relative and
dimensionless absolute tolerances $0.05\epsilon$, where the default
$\epsilon=10^{-10}$. Estimated errors above
$\epsilon\max(1,|I|)$ are rejected. All evaluated $q$ and $g$ must be finite
and positive. A 65-node initial table uses $s_i=s_g(i/64)^4$ to cluster near
the axis. A monotone piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant (PCHIP) represents
$g$. Independent midpoint quadratures identify intervals for bisection;
quadratures at unchanged locations are cached. Midpoint relative error is
measured against $\max(|g|,10^{-8}\max_i g_i)$. Refinement stops when every
midpoint error is at most $\epsilon$, with limits of 120 passes and 262145
nodes. Failure to converge is reported, rather than reducing accuracy silently.

Integrating the piecewise cubic gives a continuous flux function. Positivity
of the shape-preserving interpolant makes flux strictly increasing off the
axis. Bracketed Brent solves in $s$ invert flux, with relative tolerance
$10^{-14}$ and absolute tolerance $10^{-14}s_g$. The inverse is restricted
to the physical interval. The axis has $\psi'(0)=0$.

\section{Inverting the R--Z map}
For a requested physical point set
\begin{equation}
v=(Z-\Za)/\kappa,\qquad u=r\cos\theta,\qquad
r=\sqrt{u^2+v^2},\qquad \beta=\eta v/r.
\end{equation}
The scalar equation is
\begin{equation}
R=\Ra-\frac{A(u^2+v^2)}{2\Ra}+u\cos\beta-v\sin\beta.
\end{equation}
At the origin the ratio $v/r$ is defined as zero. For $r>0$,
\begin{equation}
\beta_u=-\eta vu/r^3,\qquad
R_u=\cos\beta-Au/\Ra-(u\sin\beta+v\cos\beta)\beta_u.
\end{equation}
Symmetric brackets start at $u=\pm r_g$ and expand by a factor of 1.5 as
needed, at most 12 times. The derivative is checked at 65 locations across
each bracket; a nonpositive derivative rejects a folded branch. Fifty
vectorized bisections solve the equation. Recover $\theta=\operatorname{atan2}(v,u)$
and verify the forward residual is at most $10^{-11}\Ra$.
No scattered interpolation or nearest-point fill is used.

\section{Coverage and rectangular continuation}
The outer required radius is $\max(a,r_{\rm requested,hi})$, or $a$ if bounds
are omitted. The physical guard is $r_g=(1+f)r_{\rm required}$, with $f=0.05$
by default. Automatic rectangular bounds enclose the guard contour with
two percent of its horizontal/vertical span added on each side. Explicit
bounds must contain the axis and have positive minimum major radius.

For $s>s_g=r_g^2$ continue the flux as
\begin{equation}
\psi(s)=\psi(s_g)+g(s_g)(s-s_g).
\end{equation}
This matches flux and its first radial derivative and stays increasing.
It supplies numerical background at rectangular corners; it does not certify
physical flux surfaces outside the guard or require q quadrature there.
The analytic coordinate inverse must remain valid at background points.

Measure distance in units of R and Z mesh spacings. Sampled LCFS and outer
required contours must be at least three cells from the guard and box edges.
Guard distances use a nearest-neighbor tree on 4097 guard points. Insufficient
clearance fails with instructions to refine the mesh or enlarge the guard/box.
All fields, certified bounds, background-node counts, and numerical settings
are recorded in the JSON companion. Optional coverage endpoints are reported
in all four radial coordinates.

\section{GEQDSK serialization}
The header uses a deterministic 48-character label followed by three I4
integers. Arrays use five E16.9 values per line; a partially filled final line
is terminated before the next array. Odd node counts from 5 to 999 are accepted.
The flux array has Z as its outer index and R as its inner (fastest) index.

and $\psi_b$ by inverting the physical radial table. A 257-point closed LCFS
polyline is written as alternating $(R,Z)$ pairs. LIMITR is zero. A temporary
file in the output directory is closed successfully before replacing the
destination. JSON records input provenance and the conventions above.

1.155593 m. These differ from its nominal outboard bounds. TCV must be read

# Miller GEQDSK generation

## Miller generator

[gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.py](gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.py) is both an importable module and a command-line
generator. It requires NumPy and SciPy. Matplotlib is optional, for `--plot`.
The implementation plan is [MILLER_EQDSK_PLAN.md](MILLER_EQDSK_PLAN.md); all formulas and numerical
methods are documented in [gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.tex](gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.tex).

From the repository root:

```bash
python3 gyrokinetic/data/eqdsk/miller/gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.py \
  gyrokinetic/data/eqdsk/miller/miller_tcv.py --output tcv_miller.geqdsk \
  --nr 257 --nz 257 --plot tcv_miller.png
```

The Python input defines `geometry={...}` and a scalar `q(R_omp)` function. All
physical parameters belong in that file; the CLI never evaluates a function
expression. `R_omp` is outboard midplane MAJOR radius in meters. Required geometry
keys are `R_axis`, `B_axis` (toroidal field), and `R_lcfs` (outboard LCFS major radius).
Defaults: `Z_axis=0`, `kappa=1`, `delta=0`, `a_shift=0`. Lengths are meters and fields
tesla. The initial convention requires positive `B_axis` and positive finite q.

Optional `R_omp_bounds=(lower,upper)` requests coverage of complete flux surfaces
for a core annulus, SOL-only simulation, or LCFS-crossing simulation. These are
NOT rectangular R bounds. The equilibrium always includes the axis and LCFS;
q must be valid all the way from the axis through the physical guard surface.
Without coverage bounds the LCFS is the outer certified surface. `--rz-bounds RMIN RMAX ZMIN ZMAX` explicitly sets the rectangular grid but does not extend
the certified physical surfaces. Rectangular corners use the documented smooth
flux continuation beyond the guard, identified in the JSON summary and plots.
The default 5-percent guard needs at least three R-Z cells of clearance; coarse
grids may require `--guard-fraction 0.25`. The node counts must be odd, 5..999.

The output includes `<output>.json`, with parameters, input provenance, flux
values, physical coverage, a conversion table, and numerical residuals. The
GEQDSK has constant `F=R_axis*B_axis` and zero pressure/current placeholders. It is
a synthetic magnetic geometry, not a Grad-Shafranov solution or a wall model.
No limiter is written. The existing tokamak IWL machinery supplies wall cuts.

Examples [miller_d3d.py](miller_d3d.py) and [miller_tcv.py](miller_tcv.py) preserve their corresponding analytic
regression inputs' surfaces and q profiles. TCV uses the actual shifted `r(x)`
endpoint surfaces, not its nominal `Rmid` bounds. Read it with `reflect=false` to
preserve `Z_axis`. LTX replaces the old rational q profile (pole at `R_omp` about
0.688328 m) with a positive exponential profile preserving LCFS q and shear.
The original script and data file remain available for comparison.

### Python API

```python
from gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk import (
  MillerGeometry, MillerEquilibrium, sample_eqdsk, write_eqdsk)
geometry = MillerGeometry(R_axis=2, B_axis=1.5, R_lcfs=2.5)
equilibrium = MillerEquilibrium(geometry, lambda R_omp: 2)
data = sample_eqdsk(equilibrium)
write_eqdsk("circle.geqdsk", equilibrium, data)
print(equilibrium.coordinates(2.4))  # R_omp, Miller r, psi, rho_psi, q.
```

### Verification

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s gyrokinetic/data/eqdsk/miller -v
make -j6 LIBRARY_TARGET=library gyrokinetic
make -j6 build/gyrokinetic/unit/ctest_gen_miller_eqdsk
./build/gyrokinetic/unit/ctest_gen_miller_eqdsk
```

reader on Python outputs as well, generate files named miller_ltx.geqdsk,
miller_d3d.geqdsk, and miller_tcv.geqdsk in one directory, then run the same C
test with `GKYL_MILLER_REFERENCE_DIR` set to that directory. Native tests always
construct their own temporary fixtures, so normal unit runs need no Python.
Both quadratic and cubic reconstructions are checked; full geometry creation
uses the existing quadratic tokamak path. LaTeX can be checked with:

```bash
pdflatex -halt-on-error -output-directory=/tmp \
  gyrokinetic/data/eqdsk/miller/gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.tex
```

## Native updater and app API

[gkyl_gen_miller_eqdsk.h](../../../zero/gkyl_gen_miller_eqdsk.h) exposes `_inew`, `_advance`, `_write`, `_get_info`,
`_psi_from_omp`, `_omp_from_psi`, `_surface`, and `_release`. Its `qprofile` callback takes

trapezoidal refinement with an explicit convergence test; radial interpolation
and the rectangular continuation follow the Python reference. It is a host
initialization updater, with no CUDA or MPI dependency.

app `lower[0]` and `upper[0]` are outboard major radii. Initialization resolves the
mutable input IN PLACE to psi bounds and `GKYL_GEOMETRY_TOKAMAK`, before creating
the configuration grid. Solver callbacks therefore receive the ordinary
tokamak coordinates (psi, alpha, parallel coordinate). They do not receive the
old analytic input's (x,y,theta). Use the updater conversions when migrating
physical profiles. Binormal extents and parallel coordinates use the existing
tokamak conventions; arbitrary analytic-input callbacks cannot be reused
without their coordinate transformations.

Generation writes `<app-name>-miller.geqdsk` unless `geometry.efit_info.filepath` is
set. Rank zero writes, collective status handling precedes reading, and the
file is retained. Generation parameters are recorded in geometry metadata.
The q callback must be deterministic and identical on all ranks. Initialization
regenerates the file, including before a restart; there is no cached-file reuse
mode. Keep the same geometry and q inputs when restarting a simulation.
The app selects IWL geometry, disables reflection, and derives R-Z search bounds.
It supports single-block 2x/3x domains, excluding the coordinate singularity at
the magnetic axis. Multiblock and language-binding APIs are not provided here.

domain surfaces are moved; mismatch beyond GEQDSK serialization precision
causes initialization to fail. `x_LCFS` is represented by the matching grid face;
the wall cutoff uses the serialized boundary flux. Core-only and SOL-only
domains have no internal split. Set ordinary species BCs: twist-shift for a
3x core annulus, and the desired open-line BCs for SOL/crossing cases. The app's
existing mixed-domain machinery handles the core part of a crossing.

advances each by one step. It uses constant profiles and a static zero field
to isolate geometry/BC initialization. Run in a scratch directory to contain
its output; MPI partitions the parallel (third configuration) direction:

```bash
make -j6 build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_miller_3x2v_p1
./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_miller_3x2v_p1 -s1
<MPI-prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 2 \
  ./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_miller_3x2v_p1 -M -e2 -s1
```

Check the returned app pointer for `NULL` after a Miller initialization failure.

zero pressure derivative. QPSI is evaluated at uniform flux nodes between zero
and $\psi_b$ by inverting the physical radial table. A 257-point closed LCFS
polyline is written as alternating $(R,Z)$ pairs. LIMITR is zero. A temporary
file in the output directory is closed successfully before replacing the
destination. JSON records input provenance and the conventions above.

normalization, and shaping. TCV's input coordinate is linear in Miller radius;

with reflection disabled to preserve its vertical offset.

results; no turbulence simulation is needed for this generator validation.

meshes and the supplied device inputs. Maximum errors on sampled simulation

# Miller GEQDSK generation

## Miller generator

[gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.py](gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.py) is both an importable module and a command-line
generator. It requires NumPy and SciPy. Matplotlib is optional, for `--plot`.
The implementation plan is [MILLER_EQDSK_PLAN.md](MILLER_EQDSK_PLAN.md); all formulas and numerical
methods are documented in [gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.tex](gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.tex).

From the repository root:

```bash
python3 gyrokinetic/data/eqdsk/miller/gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.py \
  gyrokinetic/data/eqdsk/miller/miller_tcv.py --output tcv_miller.geqdsk \
  --nr 257 --nz 257 --plot tcv_miller.png
```

The Python input defines `geometry={...}` and a scalar `q(R_omp)` function. All
physical parameters belong in that file; the CLI never evaluates a function
expression. `R_omp` is outboard midplane MAJOR radius in meters. Required geometry
keys are `R_axis`, `B_axis` (toroidal field), and `R_lcfs` (outboard LCFS major radius).
Defaults: `Z_axis=0`, `kappa=1`, `delta=0`, `a_shift=0`. Lengths are meters and fields
tesla. The initial convention requires positive `B_axis` and positive finite q.

Optional `R_omp_bounds=(lower,upper)` requests coverage of complete flux surfaces
for a core annulus, SOL-only simulation, or LCFS-crossing simulation. These are
NOT rectangular R bounds. The equilibrium always includes the axis and LCFS;
q must be valid all the way from the axis through the physical guard surface.
Without coverage bounds the LCFS is the outer certified surface. `--rz-bounds RMIN RMAX ZMIN ZMAX` explicitly sets the rectangular grid but does not extend
the certified physical surfaces. Rectangular corners use the documented smooth
flux continuation beyond the guard, identified in the JSON summary and plots.
The default 5-percent guard needs at least three R-Z cells of clearance; coarse
grids may require `--guard-fraction 0.25`. The node counts must be odd, 5..999.

The output includes `<output>.json`, with parameters, input provenance, flux
values, physical coverage, a conversion table, and numerical residuals. The
GEQDSK has constant `F=R_axis*B_axis` and zero pressure/current placeholders. It is
a synthetic magnetic geometry, not a Grad-Shafranov solution or a wall model.
No limiter is written. The existing tokamak IWL machinery supplies wall cuts.

Examples [miller_d3d.py](miller_d3d.py) and [miller_tcv.py](miller_tcv.py) preserve their corresponding analytic
regression inputs' surfaces and q profiles. TCV uses the actual shifted `r(x)`
endpoint surfaces, not its nominal `Rmid` bounds. Read it with `reflect=false` to
preserve `Z_axis`. LTX replaces the old rational q profile (pole at `R_omp` about
0.688328 m) with a positive exponential profile preserving LCFS q and shear.
The original script and data file remain available for comparison.

### Python API

```python
from gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk import (
  MillerGeometry, MillerEquilibrium, sample_eqdsk, write_eqdsk)
geometry = MillerGeometry(R_axis=2, B_axis=1.5, R_lcfs=2.5)
equilibrium = MillerEquilibrium(geometry, lambda R_omp: 2)
data = sample_eqdsk(equilibrium)
write_eqdsk("circle.geqdsk", equilibrium, data)
print(equilibrium.coordinates(2.4))  # R_omp, Miller r, psi, rho_psi, q.
```

### Verification

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s gyrokinetic/data/eqdsk/miller -v
make -j6 LIBRARY_TARGET=library gyrokinetic
make -j6 build/gyrokinetic/unit/ctest_gen_miller_eqdsk
./build/gyrokinetic/unit/ctest_gen_miller_eqdsk
```

reader on Python outputs as well, generate files named miller_ltx.geqdsk,
miller_d3d.geqdsk, and miller_tcv.geqdsk in one directory, then run the same C
test with `GKYL_MILLER_REFERENCE_DIR` set to that directory. Native tests always
construct their own temporary fixtures, so normal unit runs need no Python.
Both quadratic and cubic reconstructions are checked; full geometry creation
uses the existing quadratic tokamak path. LaTeX can be checked with:

```bash
pdflatex -halt-on-error -output-directory=/tmp \
  gyrokinetic/data/eqdsk/miller/gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.tex
```

## Native updater and app API

[gkyl_gen_miller_eqdsk.h](../../../zero/gkyl_gen_miller_eqdsk.h) exposes `_inew`, `_advance`, `_write`, `_get_info`,
`_psi_from_omp`, `_omp_from_psi`, `_surface`, and `_release`. Its `qprofile` callback takes

trapezoidal refinement with an explicit convergence test; radial interpolation
and the rectangular continuation follow the Python reference. It is a host
initialization updater, with no CUDA or MPI dependency.

```bash
make -j6 build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_miller_3x2v_p1
./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_miller_3x2v_p1 -s1
<MPI-prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 2 \
  ./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_miller_3x2v_p1 -M -e2 -s1
```

\section{Purpose, inputs, and conventions}
The module \texttt{gkeyll\_gen\_miller\_eqdsk.py} constructs a synthetic
axisymmetric magnetic geometry for the existing Gkeyll tokamak reader.

The GEQDSK pressure, pressure derivative, and current fields are zero
placeholders; the physical wall is not specified.

Lengths are in meters and magnetic fields in tesla. The flux $\psi$ is poloidal

$B_{\rm axis}$ and $q$ and flux increasing outward. The input function
$q(\Romp)$ takes the major radius at the outboard midplane, in meters.
The Miller surface label $r$ is a minor radius, whereas $R$ is the cylindrical
major radius at an arbitrary poloidal position.

Required parameters are $\Ra$, $B_{\rm axis}$, and the outboard LCFS major
radius. Defaults are $\Za=0$, $\kappa=1$, $\delta=0$, and $A=0$, where
$A$ denotes \texttt{a\_shift}. Optional outboard midplane bounds identify
complete flux surfaces intended for a simulation. They are independent of
the rectangular mesh bounds and do not crop the equilibrium to an annulus.
Core annuli, SOL-only regions, and LCFS-crossing regions are all possible.
Miller surfaces themselves contain no diverted X-point; the IWL infrastructure
supplies wall cuts for the open-field-line portion of a simulation.

\section{Surface map and analytic derivatives}
Define $\eta=\arcsin\delta$ and $h=\theta+\eta\sin\theta$. Then
\begin{align}
R(r,\theta)&=\Ra-\frac{Ar^2}{2\Ra}+r\cos h, &
Z(r,\theta)&=\Za+\kappa r\sin\theta,\\
R_r&=-\frac{Ar}{\Ra}+\cos h, &
R_\theta&=-r(1+\eta\cos\theta)\sin h,\\
Z_r&=\kappa\sin\theta, & Z_\theta&=\kappa r\cos\theta.
\end{align}
Let $D=R_rZ_\theta-R_\theta Z_r$. The cylindrical volume Jacobian is
$J_r=RD$. A useful regular expression is
\begin{equation}
\frac{D}{r}=\kappa\left[
\left(\cos h-\frac{Ar}{\Ra}\right)\cos\theta
+(1+\eta\cos\theta)\sin h\sin\theta\right].
\end{equation}
The implementation checks positive $R$ and $D/r$ on sampled physical surfaces,
including the limiting value at the axis. It also checks that the outboard
midplane map remains increasing. These numerical checks cannot prove validity
of an arbitrary user function between all sampled points.

At $\theta=0$,
\begin{equation}
\Romp(r)=\Ra-\frac{Ar^2}{2\Ra}+r,\qquad
\frac{d\Romp}{dr}=1-\frac{Ar}{\Ra}.
\end{equation}
For $d=\Romp-\Ra$, its stable increasing-branch inverse is
\begin{equation}
r=\frac{2d}{1+\sqrt{1-2Ad/\Ra}}.
\end{equation}
This expression includes the $A=0$ limit without cancellation. The LCFS
radius $a$ is obtained by applying it to the specified LCFS major radius.
A nonzero shift changes the horizontal surface center with radius; it is
independent of the constant vertical offset $\Za$.

Set $F=\Ra B_{\rm axis}$. In cylindrical coordinates the field convention is
\begin{equation}
B_R=-\frac{\psi_Z}{R},\qquad B_Z=\frac{\psi_R}{R},\qquad B_\phi=\frac{F}{R}.
\end{equation}
Because $\psi=\psi(r)$,
\begin{equation}

\psi_Z=-\psi'(r)\frac{R_\theta}{D},\qquad
B_p=\frac{\psi'(r)}{RD}\sqrt{R_\theta^2+Z_\theta^2}.
\end{equation}
The toroidal turns per poloidal circuit give
\begin{equation}
q(r)=\frac{F}{2\pi\psi'(r)}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{D}{R}\,d\theta.
\end{equation}
Consequently the imposed safety factor determines
\begin{equation}
\psi'(r)=\frac{F}{2\pi q(\Romp(r))}
\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{D}{R}\,d\theta.
\end{equation}
The boundary flux is $\psi_b=\psi(a)$, and
$\rho_\psi=\sqrt{\psi/\psi_b}$, including values above one in the physical SOL.
The profile must be defined from the axis through the guard, even when the
simulation begins away from the axis.

\section{Radial quadrature and interpolation}
Use $s=r^2$. With $g(s)=d\psi/ds$, the regular quadrature is
\begin{equation}
g(s)=\frac{F}{4\pi\Ra q(\Romp(\sqrt{s}))}
\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{\Ra}{R}\frac{D}{r}\,d\theta.
\end{equation}
The integrand is dimensionless and has a finite limit at $s=0$. A constant
triangularity extended to the axis can introduce $\sqrt{s}$ terms into $g$;
finiteness does not imply an analytic Taylor series in $s$ or a smooth axis

dimensionless absolute tolerances $0.05\epsilon$, where the default

v=(Z-\Za)/\kappa,\qquad u=r\cos\theta,\qquad
r=\sqrt{u^2+v^2},\qquad \beta=\eta v/r.
\end{equation}
The scalar equation is

R=\Ra-\frac{A(u^2+v^2)}{2\Ra}+u\cos\beta-v\sin\beta.
\end{equation}
At the origin the ratio $v/r$ is defined as zero. For $r>0$,
\begin{equation}
\beta_u=-\eta vu/r^3,\qquad
R_u=\cos\beta-Au/\Ra-(u\sin\beta+v\cos\beta)\beta_u.
\end{equation}
Symmetric brackets start at $u=\pm r_g$ and expand by a factor of 1.5 as

preserve `Z_axis`. LTX replaces the old rational q profile (pole at `R_omp` about
0.688328 m) with a positive exponential profile preserving LCFS q and shear.
The original script and data file remain available for comparison.

### Python API

```python
from gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk import (
  MillerGeometry, MillerEquilibrium, sample_eqdsk, write_eqdsk)
geometry = MillerGeometry(R_axis=2, B_axis=1.5, R_lcfs=2.5)
equilibrium = MillerEquilibrium(geometry, lambda R_omp: 2)
data = sample_eqdsk(equilibrium)
write_eqdsk("circle.geqdsk", equilibrium, data)
print(equilibrium.coordinates(2.4))  # R_omp, Miller r, psi, rho_psi, q.
```

### Verification

```bash

make -j6 LIBRARY_TARGET=library gyrokinetic
make -j6 build/gyrokinetic/unit/ctest_gen_miller_eqdsk
./build/gyrokinetic/unit/ctest_gen_miller_eqdsk
```

reader on Python outputs as well, generate files named miller_ltx.geqdsk,
miller_d3d.geqdsk, and miller_tcv.geqdsk in one directory, then run the same C
test with `GKYL_MILLER_REFERENCE_DIR` set to that directory. Native tests always
construct their own temporary fixtures, so normal unit runs need no Python.
Both quadratic and cubic reconstructions are checked; full geometry creation
uses the existing quadratic tokamak path. LaTeX can be checked with:

```bash

  gyrokinetic/data/eqdsk/miller/gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.tex
```

## Native updater and app API

[gkyl_gen_miller_eqdsk.h](../../../zero/gkyl_gen_miller_eqdsk.h) exposes `_inew`, `_advance`, `_write`, `_get_info`,
`_psi_from_omp`, `_omp_from_psi`, `_surface`, and `_release`. Its `qprofile` callback takes
`(double R_omp, void *ctx)`. The native angular quadrature uses periodic
trapezoidal refinement with an explicit convergence test; radial interpolation
and the rectangular continuation follow the Python reference. It is a host
initialization updater, with no CUDA or MPI dependency.

The app accepts `geometry.geometry_id=GKYL_GEOMETRY_MILLER` and parameters in
`geometry.miller_grid_info`, of type `struct gkyl_gen_miller_eqdsk_inp`. In this mode
app `lower[0]` and `upper[0]` are outboard major radii. Initialization resolves the
mutable input IN PLACE to psi bounds and `GKYL_GEOMETRY_TOKAMAK`, before creating
the configuration grid. Solver callbacks therefore receive the ordinary
tokamak coordinates (psi, alpha, parallel coordinate). They do not receive the
old analytic input's (x,y,theta). Use the updater conversions when migrating
physical profiles. Binormal extents and parallel coordinates use the existing
tokamak conventions; arbitrary analytic-input callbacks cannot be reused
without their coordinate transformations.

Generation writes `<app-name>-miller.geqdsk` unless `geometry.efit_info.filepath` is
set. Rank zero writes, collective status handling precedes reading, and the
file is retained. Generation parameters are recorded in geometry metadata.
The q callback must be deterministic and identical on all ranks. Initialization
regenerates the file, including before a restart; there is no cached-file reuse
mode. Keep the same geometry and q inputs when restarting a simulation.
The app selects IWL geometry, disables reflection, and derives R-Z search bounds.
It supports single-block 2x/3x domains, excluding the coordinate singularity at
the magnetic axis. Multiblock and language-binding APIs are not provided here.

An LCFS crossing sets `has_LCFS` and must align with a psi cell face. No requested
domain surfaces are moved; mismatch beyond GEQDSK serialization precision
causes initialization to fail. `x_LCFS` is represented by the matching grid face;
the wall cutoff uses the serialized boundary flux. Core-only and SOL-only
domains have no internal split. Set ordinary species BCs: twist-shift for a
3x core annulus, and the desired open-line BCs for SOL/crossing cases. The app's
existing mixed-domain machinery handles the core part of a crossing.

The focused regression `rt_gk_miller_3x2v_p1` constructs all three domains and
advances each by one step. It uses constant profiles and a static zero field
to isolate geometry/BC initialization. Run in a scratch directory to contain
its output; MPI partitions the parallel (third configuration) direction:

```bash

./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_miller_3x2v_p1 -s1
<MPI-prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 2 \
  ./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_miller_3x2v_p1 -M -e2 -s1
```

Check the returned app pointer for `NULL` after a Miller initialization failure.
\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb,booktabs,geometry,hyperref}
\geometry{margin=1in}
\title{Synthetic Miller GEQDSK generation in Gkeyll}
\author{Gkeyll}
\date{}
\newcommand{\Ra}{R_{\mathrm{axis}}}
\newcommand{\Za}{Z_{\mathrm{axis}}}
\newcommand{\Romp}{R_{\mathrm{omp}}}
\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section{Purpose, inputs, and conventions}
The module \texttt{gkeyll\_gen\_miller\_eqdsk.py} constructs a synthetic
axisymmetric magnetic geometry for the existing Gkeyll tokamak reader.
Prescribed surfaces and safety factor determine poloidal flux, with constant
$F=RB_\phi$. These choices do not in general solve the Grad--Shafranov equation.
The GEQDSK pressure, pressure derivative, and current fields are zero
placeholders; the physical wall is not specified.

Lengths are in meters and magnetic fields in tesla. The flux $\psi$ is poloidal
flux divided by $2\pi$, in Wb/radian. We set $\psi_{\rm axis}=0$, with positive
$B_{\rm axis}$ and $q$ and flux increasing outward. The input function
$q(\Romp)$ takes the major radius at the outboard midplane, in meters.
The Miller surface label $r$ is a minor radius, whereas $R$ is the cylindrical
major radius at an arbitrary poloidal position.

Required parameters are $\Ra$, $B_{\rm axis}$, and the outboard LCFS major
radius. Defaults are $\Za=0$, $\kappa=1$, $\delta=0$, and $A=0$, where
$A$ denotes \texttt{a\_shift}. Optional outboard midplane bounds identify
complete flux surfaces intended for a simulation. They are independent of
the rectangular mesh bounds and do not crop the equilibrium to an annulus.
Core annuli, SOL-only regions, and LCFS-crossing regions are all possible.
Miller surfaces themselves contain no diverted X-point; the IWL infrastructure
supplies wall cuts for the open-field-line portion of a simulation.

\section{Surface map and analytic derivatives}
Define $\eta=\arcsin\delta$ and $h=\theta+\eta\sin\theta$. Then
\begin{align}
R(r,\theta)&=\Ra-\frac{Ar^2}{2\Ra}+r\cos h, &
Z(r,\theta)&=\Za+\kappa r\sin\theta,\\
R_r&=-\frac{Ar}{\Ra}+\cos h, &
R_\theta&=-r(1+\eta\cos\theta)\sin h,\\
Z_r&=\kappa\sin\theta, & Z_\theta&=\kappa r\cos\theta.
\end{align}
Let $D=R_rZ_\theta-R_\theta Z_r$. The cylindrical volume Jacobian is
$J_r=RD$. A useful regular expression is
\begin{equation}
\frac{D}{r}=\kappa\left[
\left(\cos h-\frac{Ar}{\Ra}\right)\cos\theta
+(1+\eta\cos\theta)\sin h\sin\theta\right].
\end{equation}
The implementation checks positive $R$ and $D/r$ on sampled physical surfaces,
including the limiting value at the axis. It also checks that the outboard
midplane map remains increasing. These numerical checks cannot prove validity
of an arbitrary user function between all sampled points.

At $\theta=0$,
\begin{equation}
\Romp(r)=\Ra-\frac{Ar^2}{2\Ra}+r,\qquad
\frac{d\Romp}{dr}=1-\frac{Ar}{\Ra}.
\end{equation}
For $d=\Romp-\Ra$, its stable increasing-branch inverse is
\begin{equation}
r=\frac{2d}{1+\sqrt{1-2Ad/\Ra}}.
\end{equation}
This expression includes the $A=0$ limit without cancellation. The LCFS
radius $a$ is obtained by applying it to the specified LCFS major radius.
A nonzero shift changes the horizontal surface center with radius; it is
independent of the constant vertical offset $\Za$.

\section{Flux, safety factor, and magnetic field}
Set $F=\Ra B_{\rm axis}$. In cylindrical coordinates the field convention is
\begin{equation}
B_R=-\frac{\psi_Z}{R},\qquad B_Z=\frac{\psi_R}{R},\qquad B_\phi=\frac{F}{R}.
\end{equation}
Because $\psi=\psi(r)$,
\begin{equation}
\psi_R=\psi'(r)\frac{Z_\theta}{D},\qquad
\psi_Z=-\psi'(r)\frac{R_\theta}{D},\qquad
B_p=\frac{\psi'(r)}{RD}\sqrt{R_\theta^2+Z_\theta^2}.
\end{equation}
The toroidal turns per poloidal circuit give
\begin{equation}
q(r)=\frac{F}{2\pi\psi'(r)}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{D}{R}\,d\theta.
\end{equation}
Consequently the imposed safety factor determines
\begin{equation}
\psi'(r)=\frac{F}{2\pi q(\Romp(r))}
\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{D}{R}\,d\theta.
\end{equation}
The boundary flux is $\psi_b=\psi(a)$, and
$\rho_\psi=\sqrt{\psi/\psi_b}$, including values above one in the physical SOL.
The profile must be defined from the axis through the guard, even when the
simulation begins away from the axis.

\section{Radial quadrature and interpolation}
Use $s=r^2$. With $g(s)=d\psi/ds$, the regular quadrature is
\begin{equation}
g(s)=\frac{F}{4\pi\Ra q(\Romp(\sqrt{s}))}
\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{\Ra}{R}\frac{D}{r}\,d\theta.
\end{equation}
The integrand is dimensionless and has a finite limit at $s=0$. A constant
triangularity extended to the axis can introduce $\sqrt{s}$ terms into $g$;
finiteness does not imply an analytic Taylor series in $s$ or a smooth axis
Hessian of $\psi(R,Z)$ for general triangular shapes.

SciPy adaptive quadrature evaluates the integral with relative and
dimensionless absolute tolerances $0.05\epsilon$, where the default
$\epsilon=10^{-10}$. Estimated errors above
$\epsilon\max(1,|I|)$ are rejected. All evaluated $q$ and $g$ must be finite
and positive. A 65-node initial table uses $s_i=s_g(i/64)^4$ to cluster near
the axis. A monotone piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant (PCHIP) represents
$g$. Independent midpoint quadratures identify intervals for bisection;
quadratures at unchanged locations are cached. Midpoint relative error is
measured against $\max(|g|,10^{-8}\max_i g_i)$. Refinement stops when every
midpoint error is at most $\epsilon$, with limits of 120 passes and 262145
nodes. Failure to converge is reported, rather than reducing accuracy silently.

Integrating the piecewise cubic gives a continuous flux function. Positivity
of the shape-preserving interpolant makes flux strictly increasing off the
axis. Bracketed Brent solves in $s$ invert flux, with relative tolerance
$10^{-14}$ and absolute tolerance $10^{-14}s_g$. The inverse is restricted
to the physical interval. The axis has $\psi'(0)=0$.

\section{Inverting the R--Z map}
For a requested physical point set
\begin{equation}
v=(Z-\Za)/\kappa,\qquad u=r\cos\theta,\qquad
r=\sqrt{u^2+v^2},\qquad \beta=\eta v/r.
\end{equation}
The scalar equation is
\begin{equation}
R=\Ra-\frac{A(u^2+v^2)}{2\Ra}+u\cos\beta-v\sin\beta.
\end{equation}
At the origin the ratio $v/r$ is defined as zero. For $r>0$,
\begin{equation}
\beta_u=-\eta vu/r^3,\qquad
R_u=\cos\beta-Au/\Ra-(u\sin\beta+v\cos\beta)\beta_u.
\end{equation}
Symmetric brackets start at $u=\pm r_g$ and expand by a factor of 1.5 as
needed, at most 12 times. The derivative is checked at 65 locations across
each bracket; a nonpositive derivative rejects a folded branch. Fifty
vectorized bisections solve the equation. Recover $\theta=\operatorname{atan2}(v,u)$
and verify the forward residual is at most $10^{-11}\Ra$.
No scattered interpolation or nearest-point fill is used.

\section{Coverage and rectangular continuation}
The outer required radius is $\max(a,r_{\rm requested,hi})$, or $a$ if bounds
are omitted. The physical guard is $r_g=(1+f)r_{\rm required}$, with $f=0.05$
by default. Automatic rectangular bounds enclose the guard contour with
two percent of its horizontal/vertical span added on each side. Explicit
bounds must contain the axis and have positive minimum major radius.

For $s>s_g=r_g^2$ continue the flux as
\begin{equation}
\psi(s)=\psi(s_g)+g(s_g)(s-s_g).
\end{equation}
This matches flux and its first radial derivative and stays increasing.
It supplies numerical background at rectangular corners; it does not certify
physical flux surfaces outside the guard or require q quadrature there.
The analytic coordinate inverse must remain valid at background points.

Measure distance in units of R and Z mesh spacings. Sampled LCFS and outer
required contours must be at least three cells from the guard and box edges.
Guard distances use a nearest-neighbor tree on 4097 guard points. Insufficient
clearance fails with instructions to refine the mesh or enlarge the guard/box.
All fields, certified bounds, background-node counts, and numerical settings
are recorded in the JSON companion. Optional coverage endpoints are reported
in all four radial coordinates.

\section{GEQDSK serialization}
The header uses a deterministic 48-character label followed by three I4
integers. Arrays use five E16.9 values per line; a partially filled final line
is terminated before the next array. Odd node counts from 5 to 999 are accepted.
The flux array has Z as its outer index and R as its inner (fastest) index.
The four one-dimensional profiles are $F$, zero pressure, zero $FF'$, and
zero pressure derivative. QPSI is evaluated at uniform flux nodes between zero
and $\psi_b$ by inverting the physical radial table. A 257-point closed LCFS
polyline is written as alternating $(R,Z)$ pairs. LIMITR is zero. A temporary
file in the output directory is closed successfully before replacing the
destination. JSON records input provenance and the conventions above.

\section{Examples and verification}
The DIII-D and TCV examples retain the source input's q polynomials, field
normalization, and shaping. TCV's input coordinate is linear in Miller radius;
its exact surfaces have outboard endpoints approximately 1.051359 and
1.155593 m. These differ from its nominal outboard bounds. TCV must be read
with reflection disabled to preserve its vertical offset.

The original LTX rational q has a pole at about 0.688328 m, inside its old
sampled range. The replacement is
\begin{equation}
q(r)=q_a\exp\left[\frac{\hat s_a}{2}\left(\frac{r^2}{a^2}-1\right)\right].
\end{equation}
It preserves $q(a)=q_a$, $[r q'/q]_{a}=\hat s_a$, positivity, and $q'(0)=0$.

For circular, unshifted, constant-q surfaces the independent reference is
\begin{equation}
\psi(r)=\frac{F}{q}\left[\Ra-\sqrt{\Ra^2-r^2}\right]
=\frac{F}{q}\frac{r^2}{\Ra+\sqrt{\Ra^2-r^2}}.
\end{equation}
Tests compare this flux and its inverse to normalized tolerance $10^{-8}$,
check analytic derivatives by finite differences, and read output with an
independent fixed-width parser and Gkeyll's EFIT reader. Rectangular refinement
uses 65, 129, and 257 nodes with sufficient guards. An independent tensor cubic
interpolant reconstructs $\nabla\psi$, $B_p$, and $B$. Contour safety factor is
checked using
\begin{equation}
q=\frac{F}{2\pi}\oint\frac{dl}{R^2B_p}.
\end{equation}
The target relative field and q error on the device simulation regions is
$10^{-3}$. Physical contours are compared before coordinate-dependent metrics.
Failure tests include invalid profiles, folds, inadequate coverage, malformed
inputs, and the original LTX pole. Run the documented tests to obtain current
results; no turbulence simulation is needed for this generator validation.

\subsection{Recorded validation}
The initial CPU validation on 21 October 2026 used $257\times257$ R--Z
meshes and the supplied device inputs. Maximum errors on sampled simulation
surfaces, using the independent tensor cubic reconstruction, were:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}
Device & $|\Delta\psi|/\psi_b$ & $|\Delta B|/B$ & $|\Delta B_p|/B_p$
       & $|\Delta q|/q$ \\
\hline
LTX   & $8.0\,10^{-9}$ & $1.8\,10^{-8}$ & $2.9\,10^{-6}$ & $5.5\,10^{-7}$ \\
DIII-D & $6.2\,10^{-9}$ & $1.6\,10^{-8}$ & $2.3\,10^{-6}$ & $4.3\,10^{-7}$ \\
TCV   & $8.9\,10^{-9}$ & $6.7\,10^{-8}$ & $6.7\,10^{-6}$ & $7.5\,10^{-8}$ \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
These are sampled errors, not global error bounds. Ten Python tests passed.
Native C tests passed for generated C and Python equilibria, including EFIT
reading, quadratic and cubic contour roots, and full quadratic tokamak geometry
construction. The native generator and its unit driver also passed AddressSanitizer
and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer; the linked Gkeyll library was not instrumented.
Existing LTX geometry and EFIT tests passed. Serial and two-rank MPI app tests
initialized and advanced core-only, SOL-only, and crossing domains and checked
collective error handling. GPU hardware and Valgrind were unavailable.

The native implementation uses the same radial model and PCHIP antiderivative.
Its angular integration doubles a periodic trapezoidal rule from 32 through
16384 points, accepting successive integrals when their difference is at most
$0.05\,\mathrm{rtol}\max(1,|I|)$. It checks guard distances by direct search over
the same 4097 samples and performs scalar bisections for rectangular inversion.
\end{document}
"}

   243	
   244	\section{Native C updater and gyrokinetic app integration}
   245	\subsection{Updater interface}
   246	The implementation is \path{gyrokinetic/zero/gen_miller_eqdsk.c}, with public
   247	header \path{gyrokinetic/zero/gkyl_gen_miller_eqdsk.h}. Functions with prefix
   248	\texttt{gkyl\_gen\_miller\_eqdsk} provide the following operations:
   249	\begin{itemize}
   250	\item \texttt{\_inew}: construct the generator and radial flux table.
   251	\item \texttt{\_advance}: sample and validate the rectangular mesh.
   252	\item \texttt{\_write}: atomically write the sampled GEQDSK file.
   253	\item \texttt{\_get\_info}: return flux and coverage metadata.
   254	\item \texttt{\_psi\_from\_omp} and \texttt{\_omp\_from\_psi}: convert
   255	  between outboard major radius and physical flux.
   256	\item \texttt{\_surface}: evaluate the Miller surface map.
   257	\item \texttt{\_release}: free the generator.
   258	\end{itemize}
   259	The \texttt{qprofile} callback has arguments
   260	\texttt{(double R\_omp, void *ctx)}. This updater runs on the host during
   261	initialization and has no CUDA or MPI dependency.
   262	
   263	The native implementation uses the same radial model and PCHIP antiderivative.
   264	Its angular integration doubles a periodic trapezoidal rule from 32 through
   265	16384 points, accepting successive integrals when their difference is at most
   266	$0.05\,\mathrm{rtol}\max(1,|I|)$. It checks guard distances by direct search over
   267	the same 4097 samples and performs scalar bisections for rectangular inversion.
   268	
   269	\subsection{App inputs and coordinate conversion}
   270	The app accepts \texttt{geometry.geometry\_id=GKYL\_GEOMETRY\_MILLER}, with
   271	parameters in \texttt{geometry.miller\_grid\_info} of type
   272	\texttt{struct gkyl\_gen\_miller\_eqdsk\_inp}. In this mode, the app's
   273	\texttt{lower[0]} and \texttt{upper[0]} are outboard major radii in meters.
   274	Initialization resolves the mutable input \emph{in place} to $\psi$ bounds
   275	and \texttt{GKYL\_GEOMETRY\_TOKAMAK} before constructing the configuration grid.
   276	Solver callbacks subsequently receive the ordinary tokamak coordinates
   277	$(\psi,\alpha,\text{parallel coordinate})$, rather than the analytic input's
   278	$(x,y,\theta)$. Use the updater conversions when migrating physical profiles.
   279	Binormal extents and parallel coordinates follow the existing tokamak
   280	conventions; analytic-input callbacks require the corresponding coordinate
   281	transformations.
   282	
   283	The output is \texttt{<app-name>-miller.geqdsk} unless
   284	\texttt{geometry.efit\_info.filepath} is set. Rank zero writes the file;
   285	collective status handling and synchronization precede reading it. The file
   286	is retained, and generation parameters are recorded in geometry metadata.
   287	The $q$ callback must be deterministic and identical on all ranks.

name: code_style
description: Gkeyll's C/C++/CUDA code style is enforced by clang-format. Use when writing or editing any .c/.h/.cpp/.hpp/.cu/.cuh file, to know how to format it and which files must never be reformatted. Also use when writing or editing python scripts.
user-invocable: true

# Instructions

* Operate relative to the repo root (detect via `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).

# Code style

The style itself (indentation, brace placement, spacing, etc.) is defined by the
root `.clang-format` file plus one rule in `ci/format.py` (designated-initializer
layout, see below). Don't try to memorize or restate those rules -- just run the
formatter and let it decide:

```
python3 ci/format.py <file>...
```

Do not run bare `clang-format -i`: it packs designated initializers back onto one
line. `ci/format.py` needs clang-format 18.1.8 on PATH (`pip install clang-format==18.1.8`).

A `pre-commit` hook runs this automatically on commit, and CI (`.github/workflows/format-check.yml`)
double-checks on push/PR, so a file that hasn't been run through clang-format will
get reformatted or flagged regardless.

## The rules the config file can't express: never format `ker/` or `core/minus/`

Two kinds of files must never be run through clang-format, and never hand-formatted
to "match" the style either -- leave them exactly as they are:

- Any path matching `*/ker/*` (e.g. `core/ker/`, `gyrokinetic/ker/`) contains
  auto-generated DG kernel code (see `gkeyll_guide`'s note on `ker/`: generated with
  Maxima, never hand-edited).
- Anything under `core/minus/` is a vendored third-party library (e.g. sqlite3,
  kann, pcg_basic, STC), not Gkeyll's own code.

The pre-commit hook and CI already exclude both for this reason.

## Designated initializers: the script decides, not the trailing comma

A designated initializer that fits on one line stays on one line. One that does
not gets one member per line, first member below the `{`, closing `}` on its own
line. `ci/format.py` enforces this by stripping every trailing comma, running
clang-format, re-adding a trailing comma to each list that did not fit, and running
clang-format again. So don't add or remove trailing commas to steer the layout;
write the list any way you like and run the script.

## Two conventions the formatter enforces that you should know when reading code

- Every function *definition* has its return type on its own line, so
  `grep '^gkyl_foo('` finds the definition. Declarations keep the type on the same line.
- `case` labels are indented one level inside `switch`.

# Python style

Use the following style rules to format Python.

- Use 2-spaces instead of indents, 4-spaces, or 4-space indents.
"""Exact surfaces of rt_gk_tcv_iwl_adapt_source_3x2v_p1.c, including shift."""
import math

geometry = dict(R_axis=0.8867856264, Z_axis=0.1414361745, B_axis=1.4,
                R_lcfs=1.0870056099999, kappa=1.4, delta=-0.38, a_shift=0.5)
offset = geometry["R_lcfs"]-geometry["R_axis"]
a = 2*offset/(1+math.sqrt(1-2*geometry["a_shift"]*offset/geometry["R_axis"]))


def R_omp(r):
  # Map minor radius r [m] to outboard midplane major radius [m],
  # including the quadratic Shafranov shift of the flux-surface center.
  return geometry["R_axis"]-geometry["a_shift"]*r*r/(2*geometry["R_axis"])+r


R_omp_bounds = (R_omp(a-0.04), R_omp(a+0.08))


def q(R_omp):
  # Safety factor as a function of outboard major radius [m].
  return ((497.3420166252413*R_omp-1408.736172826569)*R_omp
          + 1331.4134861681464)*R_omp-419.00692601227627
# Miller GEQDSK generation

## Miller generator

[gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.py](gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.py) is both an importable module and a command-line
generator. It requires NumPy and SciPy. Matplotlib is optional, for `--plot`.
The implementation plan is [MILLER_EQDSK_PLAN.md](MILLER_EQDSK_PLAN.md); all formulas and numerical
methods are documented in [gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.tex](gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.tex).

From the repository root:

```bash
python3 gyrokinetic/data/eqdsk/miller/gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk.py \
  gyrokinetic/data/eqdsk/miller/miller_tcv.py --output tcv_miller.geqdsk \
  --nr 257 --nz 257 --plot tcv_miller.png
```

The Python input defines `geometry={...}` and a scalar `q(R_omp)` function. All
physical parameters belong in that file; the CLI never evaluates a function
expression. `R_omp` is outboard midplane MAJOR radius in meters. Required geometry
keys are `R_axis`, `B_axis` (toroidal field), and `R_lcfs` (outboard LCFS major radius).
Defaults: `Z_axis=0`, `kappa=1`, `delta=0`, `a_shift=0`. Lengths are meters and fields
tesla. The initial convention requires positive `B_axis` and positive finite q.

Optional `R_omp_bounds=(lower,upper)` requests coverage of complete flux surfaces
for a core annulus, SOL-only simulation, or LCFS-crossing simulation. These are
NOT rectangular R bounds. The equilibrium always includes the axis and LCFS;
q must be valid all the way from the axis through the physical guard surface.
Without coverage bounds the LCFS is the outer certified surface. `--rz-bounds RMIN RMAX ZMIN ZMAX` explicitly sets the rectangular grid but does not extend
the certified physical surfaces. Rectangular corners use the documented smooth
flux continuation beyond the guard, identified in the JSON summary and plots.
The default 5-percent guard needs at least three R-Z cells of clearance; coarse
grids may require `--guard-fraction 0.25`. The node counts must be odd, 5..999.

The output includes `<output>.json`, with parameters, input provenance, flux
values, physical coverage, a conversion table, and numerical residuals. The
GEQDSK has constant `F=R_axis*B_axis` and zero pressure/current placeholders. It is
a synthetic magnetic geometry, not a Grad-Shafranov solution or a wall model.
No limiter is written.

Examples [miller_d3d.py](miller_d3d.py) and [miller_tcv.py](miller_tcv.py) provide
DIII-D and TCV shaping and q profiles. TCV includes a vertical offset and uses
the shifted `R_omp(r)` mapping to specify its coverage endpoints.
[miller_ltx.py](miller_ltx.py) replaces the old rational q profile (pole at
`R_omp` about 0.688328 m) with a positive exponential profile preserving LCFS
q and shear.

### Python API

```python
from gkeyll_gen_miller_eqdsk import (
  MillerGeometry, MillerEquilibrium, sample_eqdsk, write_eqdsk)
geometry = MillerGeometry(R_axis=2, B_axis=1.5, R_lcfs=2.5)
equilibrium = MillerEquilibrium(geometry, lambda R_omp: 2)
data = sample_eqdsk(equilibrium)
write_eqdsk("circle.geqdsk", equilibrium, data)
print(equilibrium.coordinates(2.4))  # R_omp, Miller r, psi, rho_psi, q.
```

### Verification

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s gyrokinetic/data/eqdsk/miller -v
```

The Python tests check analytic flux, coordinate conversions, GEQDSK formatting,
field reconstruction, mesh refinement, domain coverage, and invalid inputs.

-  """Constant shaping and quadratic surface-center shift, in SI units."""
+  """Describe a family of axisymmetric Miller flux surfaces and its toroidal field.
+
+  R_axis and Z_axis locate the magnetic axis [m]; B_axis is the toroidal field
+  there [T]. R_lcfs specifies the LCFS by its outboard midplane major radius [m].
+  The dimensionless elongation kappa and triangularity delta are constant across
+  surfaces. The dimensionless a_shift sets the radial displacement of each
+  surface center: R_center(r) = R_axis - a_shift*r**2/(2*R_axis).
+
+  Surfaces are labeled by Miller minor radius r [m] and poloidal angle theta
+  [rad], with theta=0 at the outboard midplane. Methods evaluate R(r,theta),
+  Z(r,theta), their derivatives, the Jacobian factor, and conversions between
+  r and outboard major radius. The toroidal field is B_phi=R_axis*B_axis/R.
+  MillerEquilibrium combines this immutable geometry with a q profile to
+  construct the poloidal flux and magnetic field.

name: code_style
description: Gkeyll's C/C++/CUDA code style is enforced by clang-format. Use when writing or editing any .c/.h/.cpp/.hpp/.cu/.cuh file, to know how to format it and which files must never be reformatted. Also use when writing or editing python scripts.
user-invocable: true
---

# Instructions

* Operate relative to the repo root (detect via `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).

# Code style

The style itself (indentation, brace placement, spacing, etc.) is defined by the
root `.clang-format` file plus one rule in `ci/format.py` (designated-initializer
layout, see below). Don't try to memorize or restate those rules -- just run the
formatter and let it decide:

```
python3 ci/format.py <file>...
```

Do not run bare `clang-format -i`: it packs designated initializers back onto one
line. `ci/format.py` needs clang-format 18.1.8 on PATH (`pip install clang-format==18.1.8`).

A `pre-commit` hook runs this automatically on commit, and CI (`.github/workflows/format-check.yml`)
double-checks on push/PR, so a file that hasn't been run through clang-format will
get reformatted or flagged regardless.

## The rules the config file can't express: never format `ker/` or `core/minus/`

Two kinds of files must never be run through clang-format, and never hand-formatted
to "match" the style either -- leave them exactly as they are:

- Any path matching `*/ker/*` (e.g. `core/ker/`, `gyrokinetic/ker/`) contains
  auto-generated DG kernel code (see `gkeyll_guide`'s note on `ker/`: generated with
  Maxima, never hand-edited).
- Anything under `core/minus/` is a vendored third-party library (e.g. sqlite3,
  kann, pcg_basic, STC), not Gkeyll's own code.

The pre-commit hook and CI already exclude both for this reason.

## Designated initializers: the script decides, not the trailing comma

A designated initializer that fits on one line stays on one line. One that does
not gets one member per line, first member below the `{`, closing `}` on its own
line. `ci/format.py` enforces this by stripping every trailing comma, running
clang-format, re-adding a trailing comma to each list that did not fit, and running
clang-format again. So don't add or remove trailing commas to steer the layout;
write the list any way you like and run the script.

## Two conventions the formatter enforces that you should know when reading code

- Every function *definition* has its return type on its own line, so
  `grep '^gkyl_foo('` finds the definition. Declarations keep the type on the same line.
- `case` labels are indented one level inside `switch`.

# Python style

Use the following style rules to format Python.

- Use 2-spaces instead of indents, 4-spaces, or 4-space indents.
---
name: testing-and-verification
description: How to run and write Gkeyll unit and regression tests, as well as performing memory checks. Use when testing changes and verifying that changes didn't break the code or change simulation results.
---

# Instructions

* Unit tests only test the /zero layer. Regression tests test the /app layer.
* Unit tests are focused on particular /zero modules and bear the same name as the module they test.
  For example, `core/unit/ctest_array.c` tests the `core/zero/array.c` module.
* Unit tests should be modular, test only what is necessary, and be simple.
* Only test code that you understand completely.
* For code changes, run relevant unit tests and focused regression tests when
  simulation behavior is affected. Choose tests based on the changed component.
* Do not run the entire regression suite unless you are asked to; it can take a long time.
  Use the task's scope and available resources to choose the suitable testing scope.
* For documentation or agent configuration changes, validate the changed files
  and references; solver tests and memory checks are unnecessary.
* Report what was checked and any checks that could not run. If required context
  is missing or unreadable, report the exact path rather than silently skipping it.

# Running unit tests

Operate relative to the repository root (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).

In order to run all Gkeyll unit tests:
1. Compile all unit tests; see [compilation](../compiling/SKILL.md).
2. Run all unit tests with
```sh
make -j"$NPROC" unit-run
```

In order to run all unit tests for a specific solver, e.g. gyrokinetic:
1. Compile all unit tests for that solver; see [compilation](../compiling/SKILL.md).
2. Run all unit tests for that solver, e.g. for gyrokinetic use
```sh
make -j"$NPROC" gyrokinetic-unit-run
```

One can also compile and run a single unit test of interest. Simply:
1. Compile the unit; see [compilation](../compiling/SKILL.md).
2. Run the executable from the repository root:
For example, in order to run `core/unit/ctest_array.c` do

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" ./build/core/unit/ctest_array
./build/core/unit/ctest_array
```

If the Gkeyll was build on a CPU-only machine or without GPU support, unit tests will simply ignore
GPU tests (via pre-processor if-statements). When running on a machine with a supported GPU, and if
Gkeyll is configured to build GPU code, running these tests will automatically run the corresponding
GPU tests. If a GPU is not available but Gkeyll was built to use GPUs, the GPU tests may simply fail
or exit (e.g. due to GPU memory allocation errors).

### Parallel unit tests

There are a few parallel unit tests that use MPI, whose names begin with `mctest`. These tests are
compiled the same way as serial tests, but must be run with the appropriate MPI execution command.

For example if Gkeyll was built and configured with the MPI in `gkylsoft/openmpi/`, then a parallel
unit test (for example `mctest_mpi_comm.c`) may be run with

```sh
<mpi_install_prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 4 build/core/unit/mctest_mpi_comm
```

# Running regression tests

## C regression tests

Regression tests written in C and located in `creg/` directories need to be compiled first,
see [compilation](../compiling/SKILL.md).

Once compiled the regression test may be run serially with, for
`gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1.c` for example:
```sh
./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1
```

See 
```sh
./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -h
```
for command line arguments that may be available (not all are actually supported). For
example, the following command
```sh
./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -s1
```
limits the regression to a one-step smoke test.

CUDA builds place the executable in `cuda-build/` instead of `build/`, and regression tests use `-g`
to indicate GPU execution.

## Parallel regression tests

Regression executables take the `-M` command line argument to indicate a parallel run (requiring
MPI). The flags `-c X -d Y -e Z` specify that the first, second and third configuration-space
dimensions are to be subdivided amongs X, Y and Z MPI processes, respecitively. The product `X*Y*Z`
must match the number of cores available for this run. If one of `-c`, `-d` or `-e` is not given,
it is assumed to be 1.

For example, we may run `gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1` using 2 cores in the second
dimension with
```sh
<mpi_install_prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 2 ./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -M -d 2
```

For gyrokinetic partition restrictions and an example, read
[gyrokinetic-details](../gyrokinetic-details/SKILL.md).

It is also possible to run with multiple GPUs. Gkeyll's model is to match each MPI process to a
single GPU. The procedure is similar as for multiple GPUs, but the additional `-g` flag is needed.
For example, to run `gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1` using 2 GPUs in the second dimension
with
```sh
<mpi_install_prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 2 ./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -g -M -d 2
```

## Lua regression tests

Run Lua inputs using the installed executable:

```sh
<gkeyll_install_prefix>/bin/gkeyll <Lua_input_file>
```

## The runregression tool

After installing the Gkeyll library and executable one may use the `runregression` tool to run
regression tests, see

```sh
<gkeyll_install_prefix>/bin/gkeyll runregression -h
```

After configuring runregression, and having generated accepted results with
`runregression run create`, one may check the test using `runregression run check`. Note that the
flag `-r` allows check a specific test or set of tests.

The runregression tool produces SQL databases that may be examined with the `queryrdb` command,
see

```sh
<gkeyll_install_prefix>/bin/gkeyll queryrdb -h
```

# Memory checks

All code must be free of memory errors and leaks. Run the relevant CPU test
under Valgrind before committing:

```sh
valgrind --leak-check=full ./build/core/unit/ctest_array
```

For GPU changes, run the relevant executable under Compute Sanitizer:

```sh
compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck --leak-check full <executable>
```

Supply the executable's GPU options where required. Report unavailable tools
or hardware and distinguish completed checks from checks that could not run.

# Gkeyll CI system

Gkeyll has a CI system based on Jenkins which calls the aforementioned existing functionality to run
unit and regression tests. See ci/jenkins/README.md for more details.

name: code_style
description: Gkeyll's C/C++/CUDA code style is enforced by clang-format. Use when writing or editing any .c/.h/.cpp/.hpp/.cu/.cuh file, to know how to format it and which files must never be reformatted. Also use when writing or editing python scripts.
user-invocable: true
---

# Instructions

* Operate relative to the repo root (detect via `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).

# Code style

The style itself (indentation, brace placement, spacing, etc.) is defined by the
root `.clang-format` file plus one rule in `ci/format.py` (designated-initializer
layout, see below). Don't try to memorize or restate those rules -- just run the
formatter and let it decide:

```
python3 ci/format.py <file>...
```

Do not run bare `clang-format -i`: it packs designated initializers back onto one
line. `ci/format.py` needs clang-format 18.1.8 on PATH (`pip install clang-format==18.1.8`).

A `pre-commit` hook runs this automatically on commit, and CI (`.github/workflows/format-check.yml`)
double-checks on push/PR, so a file that hasn't been run through clang-format will
get reformatted or flagged regardless.

## The rules the config file can't express: never format `ker/` or `core/minus/`

Two kinds of files must never be run through clang-format, and never hand-formatted
to "match" the style either -- leave them exactly as they are:

- Any path matching `*/ker/*` (e.g. `core/ker/`, `gyrokinetic/ker/`) contains
  auto-generated DG kernel code (see `gkeyll_guide`'s note on `ker/`: generated with
  Maxima, never hand-edited).
- Anything under `core/minus/` is a vendored third-party library (e.g. sqlite3,
  kann, pcg_basic, STC), not Gkeyll's own code.

The pre-commit hook and CI already exclude both for this reason.

## Designated initializers: the script decides, not the trailing comma

A designated initializer that fits on one line stays on one line. One that does
not gets one member per line, first member below the `{`, closing `}` on its own
line. `ci/format.py` enforces this by stripping every trailing comma, running
clang-format, re-adding a trailing comma to each list that did not fit, and running
clang-format again. So don't add or remove trailing commas to steer the layout;
write the list any way you like and run the script.

## Two conventions the formatter enforces that you should know when reading code

- Every function *definition* has its return type on its own line, so
  `grep '^gkyl_foo('` finds the definition. Declarations keep the type on the same line.
- `case` labels are indented one level inside `switch`.

# Python style

Use the following style rules to format Python.

- Use 2-spaces instead of indents, 4-spaces, or 4-space indents.

name: testing-and-verification
description: How to run and write Gkeyll unit and regression tests, as well as performing memory checks. Use when testing changes and verifying that changes didn't break the code or change simulation results.
---

# Instructions

* Unit tests only test the /zero layer. Regression tests test the /app layer.
* Unit tests are focused on particular /zero modules and bear the same name as the module they test.
  For example, `core/unit/ctest_array.c` tests the `core/zero/array.c` module.
* Unit tests should be modular, test only what is necessary, and be simple.
* Only test code that you understand completely.
* For code changes, run relevant unit tests and focused regression tests when
  simulation behavior is affected. Choose tests based on the changed component.
* Do not run the entire regression suite unless you are asked to; it can take a long time.
  Use the task's scope and available resources to choose the suitable testing scope.
* For documentation or agent configuration changes, validate the changed files
  and references; solver tests and memory checks are unnecessary.
* Report what was checked and any checks that could not run. If required context
  is missing or unreadable, report the exact path rather than silently skipping it.

# Running unit tests

Operate relative to the repository root (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).

In order to run all Gkeyll unit tests:
1. Compile all unit tests; see [compilation](../compiling/SKILL.md).
2. Run all unit tests with
```sh
make -j"$NPROC" unit-run
```

In order to run all unit tests for a specific solver, e.g. gyrokinetic:
1. Compile all unit tests for that solver; see [compilation](../compiling/SKILL.md).
2. Run all unit tests for that solver, e.g. for gyrokinetic use
```sh
make -j"$NPROC" gyrokinetic-unit-run
```

One can also compile and run a single unit test of interest. Simply:
1. Compile the unit; see [compilation](../compiling/SKILL.md).
2. Run the executable from the repository root:
For example, in order to run `core/unit/ctest_array.c` do

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" ./build/core/unit/ctest_array
./build/core/unit/ctest_array
```

If the Gkeyll was build on a CPU-only machine or without GPU support, unit tests will simply ignore
GPU tests (via pre-processor if-statements). When running on a machine with a supported GPU, and if
Gkeyll is configured to build GPU code, running these tests will automatically run the corresponding
GPU tests. If a GPU is not available but Gkeyll was built to use GPUs, the GPU tests may simply fail
or exit (e.g. due to GPU memory allocation errors).

### Parallel unit tests

There are a few parallel unit tests that use MPI, whose names begin with `mctest`. These tests are
compiled the same way as serial tests, but must be run with the appropriate MPI execution command.

For example if Gkeyll was built and configured with the MPI in `gkylsoft/openmpi/`, then a parallel
unit test (for example `mctest_mpi_comm.c`) may be run with

```sh
<mpi_install_prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 4 build/core/unit/mctest_mpi_comm
```

# Running regression tests

## C regression tests

Regression tests written in C and located in `creg/` directories need to be compiled first,
see [compilation](../compiling/SKILL.md).

Once compiled the regression test may be run serially with, for
`gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1.c` for example:
```sh
./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1
```

See 
```sh
./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -h
```
for command line arguments that may be available (not all are actually supported). For
example, the following command
```sh
./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -s1
```
limits the regression to a one-step smoke test.

CUDA builds place the executable in `cuda-build/` instead of `build/`, and regression tests use `-g`
to indicate GPU execution.

## Parallel regression tests

Regression executables take the `-M` command line argument to indicate a parallel run (requiring
MPI). The flags `-c X -d Y -e Z` specify that the first, second and third configuration-space
dimensions are to be subdivided amongs X, Y and Z MPI processes, respecitively. The product `X*Y*Z`
must match the number of cores available for this run. If one of `-c`, `-d` or `-e` is not given,
it is assumed to be 1.

For example, we may run `gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1` using 2 cores in the second
dimension with
```sh
<mpi_install_prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 2 ./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -M -d 2
```

For gyrokinetic partition restrictions and an example, read
[gyrokinetic-details](../gyrokinetic-details/SKILL.md).

It is also possible to run with multiple GPUs. Gkeyll's model is to match each MPI process to a
single GPU. The procedure is similar as for multiple GPUs, but the additional `-g` flag is needed.
For example, to run `gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1` using 2 GPUs in the second dimension
with
```sh
<mpi_install_prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 2 ./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -g -M -d 2
```

## Lua regression tests

Run Lua inputs using the installed executable:

```sh
<gkeyll_install_prefix>/bin/gkeyll <Lua_input_file>
```

## The runregression tool

After installing the Gkeyll library and executable one may use the `runregression` tool to run
regression tests, see

```sh
<gkeyll_install_prefix>/bin/gkeyll runregression -h
```

After configuring runregression, and having generated accepted results with
`runregression run create`, one may check the test using `runregression run check`. Note that the
flag `-r` allows check a specific test or set of tests.

The runregression tool produces SQL databases that may be examined with the `queryrdb` command,
see

```sh
<gkeyll_install_prefix>/bin/gkeyll queryrdb -h
```

# Memory checks

All code must be free of memory errors and leaks. Run the relevant CPU test
under Valgrind before committing:

```sh
valgrind --leak-check=full ./build/core/unit/ctest_array
```

For GPU changes, run the relevant executable under Compute Sanitizer:

```sh
compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck --leak-check full <executable>
```

Supply the executable's GPU options where required. Report unavailable tools
or hardware and distinguish completed checks from checks that could not run.

# Gkeyll CI system

Gkeyll has a CI system based on Jenkins which calls the aforementioned existing functionality to run
unit and regression tests. See ci/jenkins/README.md for more details.
